title: Locally optimized variational evolution for quantum many-body systems
authors: Carolin Wille, Max Marvell, Lauren Stewart, Max Murphy, Vinul Wimalaweera, Lesley Gover, Andrew G. Green
abstract: Conventional quantum advantage in many-body dynamics is based on avoiding the simulation cost on a classical computer that arises from the extensive exponential complexity of the global wavefunction. Local observables, however, do not inherit this extensive complexity and may instead be governed by an intrinsic local complexity that is independent of the total system size. This distinction is particularly relevant in thermalising systems, where local observables lose memory of microscopic details and relax towards equilibrium values determined by only a few parameters. Here we introduce a variational time-evolution principle that exploits this distinction by replacing global-state fidelity with a cost function defined on local reduced density matrices. The resulting evolution retains coherent short-time dynamics while exploiting the simplification produced by thermalisation at later times. The concrete algorithm we propose is based on locally optimising matrix-product states and admits closed-form equations of motion analogous to the time-dependent variational principle. We show that the same variational principle has a quantum-classical counterpart, combining quantum evaluation of the local cost with an optimisation strategy robust to both shot and hardware noise. Proof-of-principle implementations on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors recover the characteristic local dynamics.
summary: This paper presents a novel variational time-evolution method, LOMPS, designed to simulate quantum many-body dynamics by optimizing local observables rather than the entire global wavefunction. By exploiting the fact that local physics can be simpler than global physics, the method achieves accurate results for both short-time coherence and long-time thermalization. The approach is demonstrated both theoretically and on superconducting quantum hardware.
main_problem: Simulating the time evolution of quantum many-body systems, which is classically intractable due to the exponential complexity of the global wavefunction.
main_result: The proposed Locally Optimized Matrix Product States (LOMPS) algorithm successfully captures both the coherent early-time dynamics and the late-time thermalization of local observables.
method: It introduces a variational time-evolution principle that replaces global fidelity with a cost function defined on local reduced density matrices, optimized using MPS techniques.
model_or_system: The study uses the transverse-field Ising model quench as a testbed, analyzing dynamics in both integrable and strongly thermalizing regimes.
key_observables: Local Loschmidt rate ($\lambda_L(t)$), local reduced density matrices ($ho_L(t)$), and entanglement entropy.
important_parameters: Patch size ($L$), bond dimension ($D$), and time step ($\Delta t$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that local observables' complexity is governed by an intrinsic local complexity independent of the total system size.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between global and local complexity evolution, the thermalization of local observables, and the implementation details of the quantum-classical hybrid algorithm on specific hardware.
paper_structure: The paper develops the LOMPS variational principle, details the classical and quantum-classical optimization procedures, and validates the method by simulating quenches on both theoretical models and actual quantum hardware.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, resource-aware numerical technique for simulating open quantum systems and thermalization dynamics by focusing computational effort only on locally accessible information.

The left and right environments of an infinite uniform (i.e., translation-invariant) MPS reduce to the left and right fixed point of the transfer matrix (see App. C 1) for details. Using the left-canonical gauge, the left-fix point is the identity and the right fixed point Renv is computed explicitly.
